reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Characterised by abrupt, severe pain around the shoulder and upper arm, followed within days to weeks by patchy weakness and wasting as the pain subsides
The distribution is often patchy and does not conform to a single nerve or root, reflecting involvement of individual nerves or plexus branches
The long thoracic nerve is frequently affected, producing scapular winging, and the anterior interosseous and suprascapular nerves are also commonly involved
Often follows an antecedent trigger such as infection, immunisation, surgery, or physical stress
Sensory symptoms are usually less prominent than the motor deficit and the early pain
A hereditary recurrent form exists (linked to SEPT9), so a family history and recurrent episodes should be explored
Diagnosis is largely clinical, supported by electromyography showing multifocal denervation, with imaging used to exclude structural or compressive lesions
Management is mainly supportive with analgesia and physiotherapy, as most patients recover over months
reference.pathophysiology: Brachial neuritis (neuralgic amyotrophy) is thought to be an immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of the brachial plexus and its branches, often triggered by antecedent infection, vaccination, surgery, or other immunological stressors. Inflammation causes multifocal axonal damage to individual nerves or fascicles, sometimes with focal nerve constrictions or torsions demonstrable on high-resolution imaging. The predominantly axonal injury explains the muscle wasting and the protracted recovery as reinnervation occurs. A hereditary form associated with SEPT9 mutations produces recurrent attacks.
additionalDifferentials: Cervical radiculopathy from disc or spondylosis
Rotator cuff disease or other primary shoulder pathology
additionalInvestigations: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies to confirm multifocal, mainly axonal involvement
MRI of the brachial plexus or high-resolution nerve ultrasound to identify constrictions and exclude structural lesions
Cervical spine MRI when radiculopathy is a competing diagnosis
Basic inflammatory and infective screen when a systemic cause is suspected
Consideration of genetic testing (SEPT9) in recurrent or familial cases
redFlags: Progressive or non-resolving deficit suggesting a compressive, neoplastic, or infiltrative plexopathy
A history of cancer or radiotherapy raising concern for malignant or radiation plexopathy
Bilateral or systemic features suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as vasculitis
Rapidly worsening weakness that warrants urgent structural imaging
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover useful function over many months to a few years, though recovery can be incomplete with residual weakness or scapular winging, and the hereditary form tends to recur.
pitfalls: Mistaking the initial severe pain for a primary shoulder or rotator cuff problem and delaying diagnosis
Confusing it with cervical radiculopathy because both cause arm pain and weakness
Overlooking scapular winging from long thoracic nerve involvement
Failing to consider a hereditary recurrent form in patients with repeated attacks
Assuming a compressive lesion and pursuing unnecessary surgery in a self-limiting inflammatory condition
management: Adequate analgesia during the severe acute phase, combining conventional analgesics with neuropathic agents such as gabapentin or amitriptyline
A course of oral corticosteroids early in the illness, which may shorten the pain phase and hasten recovery
Physiotherapy and graded rehabilitation to maintain shoulder range of movement and address scapular winging
Occupational therapy and adaptive strategies during the protracted, often incomplete recovery
Monitoring of reinnervation and function, with orthopaedic referral for tendon transfer or nerve surgery for persistent deficit
Consideration of the hereditary SEPT9-linked form, with genetic counselling in recurrent or familial cases
Multidisciplinary neurology, pain and rehabilitation input

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of brachial neuritis

nodes.text: Abrupt severe shoulder or upper arm pain, then patchy weakness and wasting over days to weeks
Red flag: progressive deficit, cancer or radiotherapy history, or bilateral or systemic features?
Escalate: urgent plexus MRI; exclude neoplastic, radiation or vasculitic plexopathy
EMG and nerve conduction studies for multifocal axonal denervation
Plexus MRI or nerve ultrasound for constrictions; cervical MRI if radiculopathy is possible
Multifocal patchy denervation without a compressive lesion?
Analgesia with neuropathic agents; early oral corticosteroids; physiotherapy
No: consider cervical radiculopathy, plexopathy or mononeuritis multiplex
Most recover over months to years; residual weakness or scapular winging is possible
